newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips says Grundig cost NLG 1.2 bn in 96.
newsitem.headline: Philips says Grundig cost NLG 1.2 bn in 96.

text.p: Philips Electronics said on Thursday its loss-making German consumer electronics unit Grundig had cost the company 1.2 billion guilders in 1996.

But Philips' finance director Dudley Eustace stressed this sum included provisions for the likely outcome of talks to quit the company's obligations to Grundig's majority shareholder, the Grundig Foundation.
"(We made) a provision for what we sincerely believe will be the outcome of the talks," Eustace told a news conference on Philips' 1996 results.

He said the 1.2 billion guilders earmarked for Grundig comprised "above the line" trading losses charged against income from operations and, below the line, an extraordinary provision for the 1996 dividend and settlement to be paid to Grundig's majority shareholders.
Philips earlier reported it had taken a gross extraordinary charge for the year of 1.85 billion guilders, of which 600 million guilders related to Grundig.
Philips is in talks to dissolve its pact with the Max Grundig Foundation under which it pays an annual dividend to the Grundig family heirs of some 45 million German marks until 2004.
Under the arrangement with Grundig, Philips had majority control over the German company, despite its minority holding.
In January Philips said it would deconsolidate Grundig and take on the role of a passive 32 percent shareholder.

The move marked a further loosening of its ties with the loss-making German electronics manufacturer, following last February's announcement it would no longer automatically make good Grundig's losses.
Philips chairman Cor Boonstra told journalists that excluding 1996, Grundig had cost the company some 1.5 billion German marks.
As such Philips strongly rejected charges that the main aim of Philips' alliance with Grundig had been to remove a competitor from the market, he said.
"I can assure you we know of cheaper ways to compete," Boonstra said.
In response to questions, Eustace said Philips had cancelled its option to purchase the 68.4 percent of Grundig stock it did not already own in 2004.
"We did not want the equity so (we) cancelled this 'genusschein' on the intercompany account between Philips and Grundig," Eustace said.
- Lien van der Leij, Amsterdam newsroom +3120 504 5000.
